You show what phase an action is in: stare per (about to start), stare + gerund (in progress), essere sul punto di, mettersi a, smettere di, continuare a, finire per and tornare a + infinitive.
The train is about to leave.
She was on the point of giving up, but then she left.
As soon as she arrived, she started cooking.
To use stare per + infinitive for an imminent action (also in the past: stavo per).
To use stare + gerund for an action in progress, in the present and the imperfetto.
To use essere sul punto di, mettersi a, scoppiare a.
To use cominciare a, continuare a, smettere di with the right preposition.
To use finire per / finire con for the final result.
To use tornare a + infinitive meaning "again".

Florence, July. Grandma Assunta, at ninety-five, has kept her promise: she's coming to Florence by train from Naples, with Rosaria. Graziella, Pietro and Signor Franco are waiting for her on the platform.
The train from Naples is about to arrive. Platform eight. I can feel it.
Signor Franco, the board says forty minutes late.
The board is lying. I was a stationmaster for thirty-five years. Trust me.
I'm dying of heat. Last night Rosaria told me Grandma was on the point of giving up.
Because she was packing her suitcase and started crying. She said that at ninety-five you don't travel.
But in August she said that at ninety-five you don't wait, you go!
Exactly. Then she stopped crying, closed the suitcase and said: "I promised. Promises are kept."
Here it is! I told you. It's coming into the station.
It's only ten minutes late! How did you know?
When a train is carrying a ninety-five-year-old grandmother, the driver always ends up going a bit faster.
"sta per arrivare" = is about to arrive
"sto morendo di caldo" = I'm dying of heat
"sul punto di" = on the point of
"si è messa a piangere" = she started crying
I was just about to call you!
Stavamo per uscire quando è arrivata.
We were about to go out when she arrived.
"Stare per" = something is going to happen right away. A stronger synonym: "essere sul punto di" (era sul punto di rinunciare = she was on the point of giving up).
Stavamo cenando quando ha squillato il telefono.
"Stare + gerund" is NOT used in the passato prossimo: NOT "sono stato mangiando". For the past use the imperfetto: stavo mangiando.
È scoppiata a ridere / a piangere.
"Mettersi a" is very Italian: "Appena arrivata, si è messa a cucinare" = as soon as she arrived, she got straight down to cooking.
Watch the prepositions: continuare A, cominciare A, mettersi A, but smettere DI, finire DI. "Finire per" = final result, often unexpected.
Dopo l’operazione è tornata a camminare.
After the operation she was able to walk again.
I'll tell you once again that…
"Tornare a" + infinitive = "again". Alternative: the prefix ri- (ripiovere, ricominciare).
She was on the point of giving up.

Da dove arriva il treno di Assunta?
Quanti minuti di ritardo indica il tabellone?
Che cosa stava facendo Assunta quando si è messa a piangere?
Perché alla fine Assunta è partita?
Con quanto ritardo arriva davvero il treno?

Assunta got off the train leaning on her stick with one hand and on Rosaria's arm with the other, slowly, step by step, while the guard waited for her on the platform with his cap in his hand, as you would for a queen. She was wearing a black dress with a white collar, her special-occasion dress, and a little straw hat she had bought specially for Florence. When she saw Graziella at the end of the platform, she stopped. For a moment it seemed she was about to say something solemn. Then she raised her stick like a flag and shouted: "Graziellina! I made it!"

The two grandmothers hugged in the middle of the platform, while travellers with suitcases flowed around them like water round a rock. Signor Franco, moved, took off his cap. Pietro was filming everything on his phone to send to Malta. Nobody said anything for a long moment. Then Assunta pulled away, looked Graziella up and down as she had done in Sorrento on the first day, and said: "You've lost weight. You're not eating enough." Graziella burst out laughing. "Look who's talking," she replied. "You weigh as much as your hat."

The journey hadn't been easy. Rosaria told the story in the car while Marco drove towards the Oltrarno. The evening before leaving, while she was packing her suitcase, Assunta had sat down on the bed and started crying. She said she was too old, that she'd be a burden, that at ninety-five you don't go travelling around Italy. Rosaria had been on the point of phoning Florence to cancel everything. Then Assunta had suddenly stopped crying, dried her eyes with her handkerchief and shut the suitcase with a sharp snap. "I promised," she had said. "And promises are kept. Even at ninety-five. Especially at ninety-five."

On the train, then, everything had happened. In Rome they had missed the connection, because the train from Naples had been arriving twenty minutes late. They had waited an hour at the station, and Assunta, instead of complaining, had started chatting with a group of young Americans sitting on the floor, to whom she told, in English invented on the spot, the story of her fisherman husband and the little fish. When the train for Florence came, the young people helped her on, carried the suitcases and asked to take a photo with her. "I reckon I've become famous in America," said Assunta with satisfaction.

The first thing she wanted to see when she arrived in Via Maggio was not her room, nor the bed Graziella had made up for her with linen sheets. It was the plaque. She stopped in front of the trattoria door, leaning on her stick, and read it aloud, slowly: "Historic Shop of Florence, since 1952." Then she touched the brass with her fingertips, as you touch a relic. "Well done," she said to Graziella. "Really well done." Graziella, who was about to say something modest, stopped and said nothing. Coming from Assunta, that "well done" was worth more than the plaque.

Then Assunta went into the trattoria, looked around, sniffed the air, and did something nobody expected of a ninety-five-year-old lady just off seven hours on a train. She took off her hat, asked for an apron and started cooking. "Tonight I'm making the ragù," she announced. "You sit down and rest." Graziella tried to protest: it was her kitchen, her trattoria, her kingdom for seventy years. But Assunta was already chopping onions, and when Assunta was chopping onions, the conversation was over.

So, for the first time since she was fifteen, Graziella spent an evening in her own trattoria sitting at a table, like a customer. At first she didn't know what to do with her hands. She kept getting up to check the sauce, and Assunta kept sending her back to her seat with a wave of the ladle. After half an hour she stopped getting up. After an hour she started chatting with Signor Franco and Bellini, who had come to dinner "by chance". At the end of the evening, glass of wine in hand, she admitted that sitting and watching someone else cook was a new experience and, all things considered, a pleasant one.

At nine sharp the video call from Malta came through. On the screen appeared Giulia, Matei and Viola, very tanned, on the terrace with the green gallarija. As soon as she saw her great-grandmother, Viola started shrieking with joy and clapping her hands. Assunta took the phone with slightly trembling hands and held it so close to her face that in Malta all they could see was her nose. "My little doll!" she said. "I'm eating in Florence! See? Great-granny is travelling!" Viola answered with her new favourite word, learned from Lina: "Grazzi!" Assunta didn't understand, but she cried anyway.

In the following days Assunta wanted to see everything. Not tourists' Florence, she said; she knew that from postcards. She wanted to see the family's Florence. So Pietro, who was about to turn thirteen and now felt like an experienced guide, organised a special tour, with the wheelchair Rosaria had hired and which Assunta used only "for long distances, that is over fifty metres". First stop: the restoration workshop, where Bellini showed her Ernesto's big iron key and Chiara explained the silk altar cloth she was working on with Doina.

There something wonderful happened. Doina and Assunta had never met. They had no language in common: Doina spoke hesitant Italian, Assunta very fast Neapolitan Italian. And yet, after five minutes, they were already embroidering the same piece of silk together, one on each side of the frame, without saying a word, as if they had done it all their lives. Chiara watched them with wet eyes. "There," she whispered to Bellini. "This is the most beautiful restoration I've ever seen. And I'm not doing anything."

Before leaving the workshop, Assunta stopped in front of Bellini, who was watching her from his corner with his hands behind his back. "You're the professor who had the little heart problem," she said. "The one from the video." Bellini made a small bow. Assunta studied him for a long time, then told him something she had never told even Rosaria. In 1943, in Naples, when she was twelve, she had been about to go into an air-raid shelter with her mother when an old painter from the neighbourhood stopped them in the street and asked for help carrying the paintings out of his church. They ended up spending the night saving the canvases instead of hiding. "The shelter was hit that night," she said softly. "The paintings saved our lives. That's why, when Giulia told me she wanted to be a restorer, I cried. It was the family debt coming home."

Bellini was left speechless, which almost never happened to him. Then he went to the drawer, took out Ernesto's 1966 diary and opened it at page forty, the one about Aldo and the San Frediano Madonna. "Then you'll understand," he said, handing it to her. Assunta read the page slowly, glasses on the tip of her nose, moving her lips. When she had finished, she looked up at Graziella, who was standing in the doorway. "Your husband carried a Madonna through the mud," she said. "I carried a San Gennaro under the bombs. I reckon our families were bound to meet." Graziella smiled. "So do I," she replied. "It just took a bit of time. Seventy years, more or less."

Second stop: the church of Santo Spirito, where Viola had been baptised in Assunta's 1934 gown. Assunta asked to be taken to the font, looked at the water for a long time and said only: "I knew that dress would come in useful again." Third stop: the house in Via Maggio, on the first floor, Viola's little room with the notches on the door frame. Pietro showed her Viola's notch, Marco's at ten, his own. Assunta took a pencil from her bag and asked if she could make one too. Pietro, hesitantly, helped her up. Assunta stood against the door, straight as a soldier, and Pietro marked her height: one metre forty-eight.

"Shorter than Viola in a few years," said Assunta, looking at the mark, and burst out laughing. Then she became serious. "Write the name," she said. "And the date. And the age. Ninety-five. So that when Viola is grown up and has forgotten me, she'll see that her great-grandmother was here, and that she was this tall." Pietro wrote in his neatest handwriting: "Assunta, 95, July." It was the lowest notch among the grown-ups', lower even than Marco's at twelve. And it was, Graziella said that evening, the tallest of them all.

On 12 July Pietro turned thirteen. The party was held at the trattoria, with two cakes: a Florentine one, Graziella's schiacciata, and a Neapolitan one, Assunta's pastiera, made in secret the night before while everyone was asleep. Pietro had to taste both and, as in Sorrento, declare a winner. He was about to answer with a diplomatic sentence when Davide, next to him, whispered: "Say they both won, otherwise it'll end in war." Pietro said it. The two grandmothers looked at each other, pretended to be offended for a second, and ended up laughing together.

Before the cake, as every year, Marco stood Pietro against the door frame for the birthday notch. This time, though, Assunta was with them, sitting on a chair by the door, watching carefully. When Marco marked the new height, Pietro's notch turned out to be exactly thirty centimetres higher than Assunta's. "One metre seventy-eight," Marco announced. "At thirteen." Assunta shook her head. "These young people today," she said. "They keep growing like grass. My husband at twenty was as tall as Pietro at ten. And he still caught the biggest fish in the gulf."

Assunta stayed in Florence for two weeks. On the last day she asked to be taken to the Ponte Vecchio at sunset, "because everyone says it's beautiful, and at ninety-five you can't put things off any longer". Pietro pushed the wheelchair, Graziella walked beside it, Rosaria and Marco behind. They stopped halfway across the bridge, in front of the river turning gold. Assunta was silent for a long time. Then she said something nobody expected. "You know, when I was packing my suitcase and started crying, it wasn't because of the journey. It was because I thought it would be the last."

Graziella took her hand. Nobody said anything. The Arno kept flowing under the bridge, as it had flowed in 1966 and as it would go on flowing after them. Then Assunta turned to Pietro and smiled. "But now I've changed my mind," she said. "It's not the last. In September my Giulia comes back from Malta, and I want to be here. And in December it's Christmas, and I want to eat your panettone, even though ours is better. So, young man, get ready. Great-granny is about to become a traveller."

The next day, at the station, Signor Franco was on the platform again, with his old stationmaster's paddle. When the train for Naples was about to leave, he raised it, as he used to, and gave the signal. The guard, a young man who had never seen anything like it, looked at him in astonishment, then smiled and gave a little military salute. From the window, Assunta waved her straw hat. Graziella stayed on the platform until the train disappeared round the bend. Then she turned to Pietro. "Let's go," she said. "We've got a trattoria to reopen. And tonight, at last, I'm cooking."

That evening, while Graziella was making ribollita for the first time in two weeks, Pietro went up to Viola's room and stopped in front of the door frame. He looked at the notches one by one, from the bottom up: Viola, two; Marco, six; Marco, ten; Assunta, ninety-five; himself, at every age. And at the top, his own, new, at thirteen. He thought that door was like a history book, written in pencil, in which time was passing without making a sound. Then he picked up his phone and sent a photo of the door frame to Malta, with a single message: "We're missing yours. Come back soon."
